_comment: The twelfth tell: sentences that instruct the reader, or that frame the subject
as something to write in an answer. `tools/voice_audit.py` reports 0 for its
eleven patterns, and that number is true of those eleven - but it is a floor,
not the truth. This file is the family that stayed:
* sentences that open with an instruction to the reader ("Read the tiers as a
division of labour, not a diagram", "Keep the two kinds of transparency
* sentences whose subject is the answer rather than the subject ("the sentence
to write in an answer is the one-line rule", "Two connections worth making
in an answer", "the distinction students lose").
Written as prose - the sentence to change, the sentence to put in its place,
which tell it retires and why - and resolved to exact markup by
`tools/voice_rewrite.py --curate`, which refuses anything that is not one place
in the file. An empty `new` deletes the sentence.
Not every imperative is a tell and none of these entries touch the ones that
are mathematics: "Consider a circle x2 + y2 = r2 inscribed in a square of side
2r", "Check that the In and Out counts add up to N before you compute the
integral" and "Every disadvantage maps onto a step" are teaching, and a pass
that removed them would be removing the subject.

edits.why: the reader does not need to be told how to read a three-tier diagram; the tiers themselves are the fact
edits.old: Read the tiers as a division of labour, not a diagram: the presentation tier holds what the user sees
edits.new: The presentation tier holds what the user sees

edits.why: a comparison whose subject is the mapping onto ten steps, not the reader's reading of it
edits.old: Read the same list against 2.1.1's ten steps and every disadvantage maps onto a step:
edits.new: Each disadvantage maps onto one of the ten steps:

edits.why: the sentence is about a marked answer and what it makes a student look like, which is not a fact about transparency
edits.old: Keep the two kinds of transparency apart, because an answer that mixes them reads as if the student has not noticed the difference.

edits.why: a heading names the two words; that they are wanted in an answer is a claim about the paper
edits.old: Two words to use precisely in an answer
edits.new: Two words to use precisely

edits.why: easy to confuse is a fact about the two properties; easy to get wrong in an answer is a fact about the marking
edits.old: Two properties of SPMD are easy to get wrong in an answer.
edits.new: Two properties of SPMD are easy to confuse.

edits.why: the three protocols are one trade whether or not the reader is told to read them that way
edits.old: Read the three protocols as one trade seen at three settings: how much buffer memory you spend to avoid waiting.
edits.new: The three protocols are one trade seen at three settings: how much buffer memory is spent to avoid waiting.

edits.why: the two phases are the content; that stating them structures an answer is strategy
edits.old: Every election algorithm has two phases, and stating them is a reliable way to structure an answer:
edits.new: Every election algorithm has two phases:

edits.why: the three message types are the content; what an answer should name is about the marking
edits.old: Three message types, and an answer should name all three:
edits.new: Three message types:

edits.why: the trade is the fact; to state it in an answer is strategy
edits.old: That is the trade to state in an answer: message cost per entry against a single object whose loss stops everything.
edits.new: That is the trade: message cost per entry against a single object whose loss stops everything.

edits.why: the one-line rule is the fact; that it is the sentence to write in an answer is about the paper
edits.old: The sentence to write in an answer is the one-line rule: CORBA's interface is defined in a neutral language
edits.new: The one-line rule: CORBA's interface is defined in a neutral language

edits.why: what the table separates is the content; that it is the skeleton of an answer is strategy
edits.old: Read the table as the skeleton of any “explain cloud computing models” answer, because it separates three things that are easy to blur together:
edits.new: The table separates three things that are easy to blur together:

edits.why: a label for the section, stripped of the aside about what students lose
edits.old: Scalability versus elasticity - the distinction students lose.
edits.new: Scalability versus elasticity.

edits.why: the four lists map the jobs whether or not the reader is told to read them as a map
edits.old: Read the four lists as a map of the jobs a provider has to staff, and notice how much of it is not computing at all.
edits.new: The four lists map the jobs a provider has to staff, and much of it is not computing at all.

edits.why: the layer names are the model's own; where they came from is not a fact about the model
edits.old: The layer names are the ones the deck uses, and the client row at the top is part of its diagram because the model is defined by what reaches the user.
edits.new: The client row at the top is part of the model, which is defined by what reaches the user.

edits.why: the fact is that virtualization is a cause; the question's wording is the paper's business
edits.old: When a question asks why cloud computing became possible, virtualization is part of the answer.
edits.new: Virtualization is one reason cloud computing became possible.

edits.why: the two lookups are the reason; that they are the answer to a question is framing
edits.old: If a question asks why memory virtualization costs performance, that is the answer - two lookups where a physical machine does one -
edits.new: Memory virtualization costs performance because of two lookups where a physical machine does one -

edits.why: one mechanism seen five times is the insight, and it stands without the claim about what turns a list into an answer
edits.old: The five are not five separate advantages; they are one mechanism seen five times, and stating that is what turns the list into an answer.
edits.new: The five are not five separate advantages; they are one mechanism seen five times.

edits.why: how to draw it is the instruction; in an answer is the framing
edits.old: How to draw it in an answer.
edits.new: How to draw it.

edits.why: the sentence is entirely about the second rule and about turning a list into an answer
edits.old: That is exactly the exercise the second rule asks for - consider the impact of the cloud on each phase - and it is what turns a list of seven words into an answer.

edits.why: the connections are between the phases, not between points of an answer
edits.old: Two connections worth making in an answer.
edits.new: Two connections between the phases.

edits.why: the technical half of the protection is the fact; the half of an answer is about the paper
edits.old: Encryption in transit, from 8.1.1, is the technical half of the answer.
edits.new: Encryption in transit is the technical half of the protection.

edits.why: the sentence carries the subject; that it is what to write in an answer is framing
edits.old: In an answer about cloud-native architecture, one sentence carries it: containers trade isolation for density
edits.new: One sentence carries cloud-native architecture: containers trade isolation for density

edits.why: the chain of roles is the content; that it answers a question is framing
edits.old: That chain is the answer to “how do containers and orchestration support cloud-native architecture”.

edits.why: a label for the definition, without the instruction about what an answer needs
edits.old: The one-line definition for an answer.
edits.new: The one-line definition.

edits.why: the sentence rates answers instead of stating what the trends cost
edits.old: An answer that names what each trend buys and what it costs is the one that reads as understanding rather than as a list.

edits.why: the two roles are complementary; whether the course's syllabus pairs them, and what half an answer needs, are not facts about the tools
edits.old: Docker answers “how does this run the same way everywhere?”; Kubernetes answers “how does it keep running, at the right size, when machines fail?” Because the course's syllabus pairs them in one sub-topic, an answer that gives only one of the two roles has answered half the question.
edits.new: Docker answers “how does this run the same way everywhere?”; Kubernetes answers “how does it keep running, at the right size, when machines fail?” The two roles are complementary, and one without the other describes half the pair.

edits.why: the Past Questions tab already carries the model answer, and the guarded pointer line is what says so
edits.old: The model answer is in the past-questions tab; the shape of it is this:
